groups.label: Read the passage and choose the paragraph that contains the information in each statement. A paragraph may be used more than once.
groups.text:
Should the University Library Stay Open All Night?

[A] Consider a fictional university facing a familiar policy choice. For most of its history, its central library closed its doors at ten in the evening. That schedule suited an earlier generation of students, who tended to study in their dormitories and came to the building mainly to borrow books. In recent years, however, the pattern of student life has shifted. Many undergraduates now treat the library as their principal workplace, arriving after dinner and staying until they are asked to leave. As a result, a campaign has grown on campus to keep the building open around the clock, at least during the weeks before examinations.

[B] The case for longer hours rests first on simple practical grounds. Students who live in crowded shared rooms often have nowhere quiet to read after the dormitory corridors fall silent, and those with part-time jobs may not be free to study until late at night. Supporters of the proposal point out that a modern university already provides lighting, heating and security for its buildings throughout the night; the marginal cost of allowing students to remain inside is therefore smaller than it first appears. To them, a library that closes just when students are most anxious to use it looks like a poor use of an expensive public resource.

[C] Opponents do not deny that late-night study is real. Their objection is that the demand is thinner than the campaign suggests. Sign-in records collected during a trial period last spring showed that between midnight and six in the morning the building rarely held more than forty people, while the average during the day exceeded eight hundred. Extending the hours for a handful of users, they argue, would divert money and staff attention from services that benefit the whole student body, such as additional daytime research assistance or a larger collection of electronic journals.

[D] Cost is not the only consideration. Running a building through the night requires more than leaving the lights on. A minimum number of trained staff must be present, security arrangements must be strengthened, and cleaning crews must adjust their schedules. University administrators have estimated that a full year of round-the-clock opening would require the equivalent of several full-time positions, money that would have to come from somewhere in an already tight budget. Critics of the plan say that this figure is rarely mentioned when the proposal is discussed in student meetings.

[E] There is also the question of safety. A library that never closes becomes, in effect, a public space at three in the morning, and universities have a duty of care toward the young people who use it. The campus safety team worries that unrestricted entry might allow people with no university connection into the building, while students leaving alone would need a reliable way home. Supporters reply that these dangers already exist for anyone who studies late in a laboratory or a computer room, and that the solution is better lighting and escort services rather than an early closing time.

[F] The campus health advisers add a further note of caution. They do not claim that an open building directly causes poor sleep. Instead, they ask whether promotional messages might make studying through the night seem like an expectation rather than an option. A student with a heavy workload may interpret the new service as a recommendation to stay longer. The advisers want any announcement to make clear that extended access is intended to accommodate different schedules, not to increase the total hours students spend studying. Their concern is therefore about how the service is presented, as well as when it is available.

[G] A quieter argument concerns the character of the library itself. A library is not merely a hall with desks in it; it is a place where books are kept, catalogued and preserved. Librarians have noted that round-the-clock opening would require the building to be occupied during the hours now used for maintenance, repair and the reshelving of returned books. Some of this work could be moved to daytime, but not all of it. Over months and years, they suggest, small delays in these tasks could damage the collections that give the library its value.

[H] The facilities team offers a way to test the proposal without committing the whole building. It suggests opening a single reading room while keeping the upper floors closed. Staff could then check whether the demand justifies the expense before considering a larger service. Access to that room would not include borrowing books, since the lending desk would remain closed. The distinction matters: a trial of study space cannot establish whether students need every library service throughout the night. A modest experiment can inform a later decision, provided its limited purpose is understood by everyone discussing the results.

[I] Students themselves are divided. In a poll conducted last term, a narrow majority supported some form of extended opening, but when asked whether they would accept a small increase in library fees to pay for it, the majority shrank sharply. Supporters of the campaign argue that this response reflects a reasonable wish to see the university spend its existing budget more carefully rather than a lack of commitment. Opponents read the same numbers as evidence that most students, when the cost is placed before them, prefer the current arrangement.

[J] What the discussion has revealed most clearly is how little anyone knows about how students actually use the building. The sign-in figures cover only those who pass through the main entrance; they say nothing about how long people stay or what they do. Before the university commits itself to a permanent change, both sides might agree that a careful study of use, cost and outcomes would be more useful than another round of speeches in the student union. Whatever the final decision, it is likely to be watched closely by other universities facing the same question.

[K] For the moment, the library continues to close at ten. A pilot scheme, in which one reading room on the ground floor will remain open until two in the morning during the four weeks before examinations, has been approved for the coming term. Its results, supporters hope, will settle the matter in their favour; its critics expect the opposite. Either way, the trial will provide the campus with something the debate has so far lacked: figures gathered on purpose, rather than impressions gathered in passing.

items.stem: During the spring trial, overnight attendance seldom exceeded forty, compared with more than eight hundred in daytime.
items.why: [C] 段给出春季试行的两个对应人数：夜间很少超过四十，白天平均超过八百。

items.stem: The author mentions buildings already supplied with lighting, heating and security at night.
items.why: 材料[B]段指出大学夜间本就为建筑提供照明、供暖和安保，因此增加开放时段的边际成本没有看上去那么大。

items.stem: Health advisers want the announcement to distinguish access for different schedules from encouragement to study for more hours.
items.why: [F] 段明确要求说明延时服务是适应不同作息，不是增加学习总时长；需同时核对宣传主体和限定目的。

items.stem: One proposal would provide a room for study while leaving the book-lending desk closed.
items.why: [H] 段同时限定只开放阅览室且借书柜台关闭；仅有阅览空间不能等同于全部图书馆服务。

items.stem: The writer suggests that the evidence about how the building is really used is currently quite limited.
items.why: 材料[J]段说讨论暴露出人们对学生实际如何使用图书馆知之甚少，签到数字只覆盖从正门进入的人。

items.stem: Some argue that spending on late hours would take resources away from services used by all students.
items.why: 材料[C]段说反对者认为延长开放会把资金和人员注意力从惠及全体学生的服务上转移走。

items.stem: A reading room will stay open until two in the morning for four weeks before examinations.
items.why: 材料[K]段说下学期将试行底层一间阅览室在考试前四周开放到凌晨两点。

items.stem: The passage points out that keeping a building open all night involves trained staff, security and cleaning adjustments.
items.why: 材料[D]段说通宵开放需要最低数量的受训员工、加强安保并调整清洁人员的时间表。

items.stem: Supporters claim that the dangers of late-night study already apply to those working in laboratories or computer rooms.
items.why: [E] 段中支持者指出实验室和机房也存在深夜离开时的风险，建议照明与护送，而非提前闭馆。

items.stem: The number of students favouring extended hours drops considerably when a fee increase is mentioned.
items.why: 材料[I]段说被问及是否接受小幅提高图书馆费用时，多数支持者的人数急剧减少。

groups.text:
The Parking Puzzle of Shared Bikes

[A] Imagine a fictional city introducing shared bicycles to connect residential streets with busy subway stations. Several operators enter the market, each placing a large fleet of brightly colored bicycles around the city. For a modest fee, a person with a smartphone can unlock a bicycle and make a short journey without owning or storing one. The arrangement promises convenient access for riders and fewer short car trips for the city. However, the location where each journey ends has not received the same attention as the ease with which it begins. That omission soon becomes central to the debate.

[B] The trouble lay precisely in that freedom. Early advertisements promised riders that they could "park anywhere", and many took the promise literally. Bicycles were left across building entrances, on tactile paving meant for blind pedestrians, in front of shop doors and in the middle of bus stops. On residential estates, piles of damaged machines sometimes blocked stairwells. Complaints from pedestrians, wheelchair users and shopkeepers rose sharply, and city governments began to see the fleets not as a green transport solution but as a new kind of street clutter.

[C] Regulators responded with designated parking areas. The city paints rectangles on the pavement and uses electronic boundaries in selected districts to determine whether bicycles have been returned to the marked zones. Riders who abandon a bike outside would, in theory, be fined or blocked from further use. The logic is simple and familiar from car parking: a shared resource should be returned to a defined place, so that it does not damage the public space it borrows. On paper, the plan appears to solve the problem at a stroke.

[D] In practice, enforcement has been uneven. A rider who is in a hurry and late for work has little incentive to walk two hundred metres to the nearest marked zone, especially when the penalty is small and the chance of being caught is lower still. Some users report that the app's location signal is imprecise, so a bicycle left correctly inside a zone is sometimes recorded as outside it, and the reverse also happens. When penalties fall on people who believe they have followed the rules, trust in the system erodes, and with it the willingness to cooperate.

[E] The operators, for their part, face a difficult arithmetic. Every bicycle must be collected, repaired and redistributed to where demand is highest, usually by van. If bicycles are scattered at random, the cost of this work rises steeply, and so does the time it takes to move a machine from a quiet street to a busy station in the morning rush. Companies that once competed almost entirely on the size of their fleets have begun to compete on the efficiency of their operations, because a bicycle that cannot be found earns nothing.

[F] The city therefore considers shifting the burden of parking from the rider to the company. Under these arrangements, operators are given a licence to run a limited number of bicycles, and in return they must guarantee that the vehicles are parked in an orderly way, remove broken ones within a set number of hours, and pay a fee for the use of public space. The advantage is that responsibility now rests with a party that has the staff, the vehicles and the data to manage it. The disadvantage is that the number of bicycles in a city is capped, which can leave users in outer districts with too few machines.

[G] Technology has offered partial help. Satellite positioning has become more accurate, and many bicycles now carry sensors that tell the company whether a machine is standing upright or lying on its side. In this scenario, some apps show riders a photograph of the exact parking spot before they ride, and require a picture of the parked bicycle before the trip is closed. These small frictions do reduce careless parking, but they also remind us that a service advertised as effortless has acquired a growing set of rules and conditions.

[H] Pedestrians have their own perspective, and it is not always heard. For an elderly person or a parent pushing a pram, a bicycle lying across a narrow pavement is not an inconvenience but an obstacle that may force them onto the road. Disability groups have pointed out that shared bicycles parked on tactile paving are especially dangerous for people who rely on those surfaces to navigate. Their argument is not that bicycle-sharing should end, but that the space it occupies should be counted and paid for, just as a shop pays for the pavement it uses for a display stand.

[I] There is also a question of fairness between riders and non-riders. The benefit of a shared bicycle goes mainly to the person who rides it, while the cost of cluttered pavements is spread across everyone who uses the street. Economists describe this as a classic case in which a private benefit creates a public burden, and they generally recommend that the user bear more of the cost, either through higher prices or through stricter rules. Yet raising prices can push casual users back to cars and buses, which is the opposite of what cities want.

[J] To explore a more local solution, suppose one district asks neighborhood committees to select parking locations after consulting residents, shopkeepers and disability groups. In this hypothetical trial, more riders return their bicycles correctly even though penalties remain unchanged. The committees discover that some previously marked areas were inconveniently placed, while useful spaces near shops had been overlooked. A neighboring district plans a different trial, offering points for correct parking, but has not yet collected results. The first trial suggests that involving affected people can improve the arrangement; it does not establish that rewards are better than penalties or that every district should use identical locations.

[K] It is tempting to conclude that the problem is simply one of better technology or stricter rules. But the deeper issue is that shared bicycles blur an old boundary. A bicycle is private property, yet when it stands on a public pavement it becomes part of the public realm. The city has always had rules for where private objects may be left, and it has always had to negotiate those rules with the people affected. The task now is to apply that old habit of negotiation to a new and faster kind of object, before the pavements fill up again.

items.stem: The author notes that fixing the position on a map is sometimes inaccurate, so bicycles correctly placed are recorded as being elsewhere.
items.why: 材料[D]段说应用定位不准，正确停在区域内的车有时被记为在区域外。

items.stem: In the imagined city, several competing operators introduce large fleets at the start of the service.
items.why: [A] 段设定几家运营商各投放大量车辆；这是虚构城市的起始情景。

items.stem: Marked pavement areas and electronic boundaries are used together in selected districts to check where bicycles are returned.
items.why: [C] 段同时提及地面矩形标线和部分区域的电子边界；电子核验只限所选区域。

items.stem: The proposed rewards trial in a neighboring district has not yet produced evidence about its effectiveness.
items.why: [J] 段说明相邻区的积分奖励试行尚未收集结果；不能把前一试行的改善移给奖励措施。

items.stem: Riders are required, in some apps, to take a picture of the bicycle after parking before the trip can be finished.
items.why: 材料[G]段说一些应用要求骑行者在结束行程前拍下停好的自行车。

items.stem: Disability groups argue that bicycle operators should account for occupied pavement space, drawing a comparison with shop displays.
items.why: [H] 段将占用人行道的单车与商店陈列架比较，主张占用空间应计入并付费；[B] 只列举堵塞问题。

items.stem: Under licensing arrangements, a company must clear away damaged vehicles within a fixed period of time.
items.why: 材料[F]段说在牌照制度下运营方须在规定小时数内移走损坏车辆。

items.stem: The point is made that a private gain places a cost on the general public, so the user should pay more.
items.why: 材料[I]段说骑行者得利而杂乱人行道的代价由所有人承担，经济学家建议使用者承担更多成本。

items.stem: The passage reports that redirecting bicycles to busy stations by van becomes more expensive when they are left scattered.
items.why: 材料[E]段说车辆散落各处时，用货车收集、维修并调运的成本急剧上升。

items.stem: In a hypothetical local trial, consultation improved parking behavior without an increase in fines.
items.why: [J] 段的假设试行同时满足征询居民意见、停放改善和罚款未变；积分奖励是另一区尚无结果的试行。
